## Formal {.unnumbered}

In the R programming language, the definition of a function diverges sharply from standard imperative languages because R is deeply rooted in functional programming and Scheme-like semantics.

In R, functions are not merely structural blocks of code or subprograms; they are first-class objects (also known as "closures") that combine an executable body with a specific lexical scope.
Here are the rigorous textbook and documentation definitions of a function within the R paradigm.

1. The Language Definition: The Three-Component Object Model
According to R’s core language architects, a function is a specific data structure of type "closure" that is composed of three distinct, inseparable parts.
Documentation Source
Manual: R Language Definition (Official Core Documentation)
Authors: R Core Team
Publisher: R Foundation for Statistical Computing
The Formal Definition
In Chapter 2 ("Objects") and Chapter 4 ("Functions"), the core documentation formalizes a function:
"R functions are first-class objects. They are of type "closure" and can be manipulated in the same way as any other object. A function object is formally defined as a list-like structure consisting of three essential components:
The Formals: The list of formal arguments (parameters) that the function accepts, which can include default values and the special ... (ellipsis) argument.
The Body: The expressions or code block that are executed when the function is evaluated.
The Environment: The specific lexical environment (scope) in which the function was created. This determines how variables inside the function are resolved."
Mathematically and structurally, R represents this object model via the primitive constructor:
Function=⟨formals,body,environment⟩
LaTeX Format
Code snippet
$\text{Function} = \langle \text{formals}, \, \text{body}, \, \text{environment} \rangle$

2. The First-Class / Closure Definition (Lexical Scoping)
Because R treats functions as first-class citizens, a function can be created anonymously, assigned to variables, passed as arguments to other functions, and returned from functions. This introduces the formal concept of a closure.

Textbook Source
Book: Advanced R (2nd Edition, 2019)
Author: Hadley Wickham
Publisher: Chapman and Hall/CRC

The Formal Definition
In Chapter 6 ("Functions") and Chapter 10 ("Functional Programming"), Wickham definitions the true nature of an R function:
"An R function is a closure, a name that reflects the fact that the function 'encloses' its environment.
When you define a function in R, it binds a pointer to the environment where it was born. This is why R functions can remember values from their parent scopes even after the parent function has finished executing. The process of calling a function involves creating a new execution environment that is temporarily nested inside the function's definition environment."

3. The Structural Reflection Properties
In R code, this rigorous definition is not hidden; it is entirely introspectable. If you have a function named f, R provides explicit primitives to extract the three components of its formal definition:
formals(f) returns the list of arguments.
body(f) returns the expression tree of the code.
environment(f) returns the pointer to its enclosing scope.
Because of this unique architecture, an anonymous function definition like function(x) x + 1 is an expression that evaluates directly to an object in memory, and assigning it to a variable (add_one <- function(x) x + 1) is simply binding that name to the function object—identical to how the value-binding assignment model works for numbers or matrices.
